opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the framing I keep coming back to is that right now the researcher is the bottleneck. The typical loop is: you have an idea, you write some code, you kick off a run, you go get coffee, you come back, you squint at some loss curves in a dashboard, you form an opinion, and you tweak something. Every step of that has a human in it, and humans are slow, they sleep, they get distracted, and frankly they're not very good at holding a hundred experiments in their head at once.

So the reorganization I'd want is to make the whole thing legible to an agent. A lot of research infrastructure today is built for humans: notebooks, Slack threads where someone says "hey, I tried this and it didn't work," tribal knowledge about which hyperparameters are cursed. None of that is accessible to an LLM. If you want to remove humans from the loop, you need the objective to be crisp and automatically measurable, the experiments to be cheap and sandboxed, and the history of what's been tried to be written down in a form a model can read and reason about.

Concretely I picture it like this: you, the human, define the arena. Here's the codebase, here's the metric, here's the compute budget, here's what you're not allowed to touch. Then you let a swarm of agents propose changes, run them, read the results, and keep a running log of what they learned, almost like a lab notebook, but one that's actually machine-readable. The human moves up a level of abstraction. You're less the person turning the knobs and more the PI, or almost the program designer: you're writing the "research org" itself, in a sense, the prompts and the structure and the evaluation, and then you're reviewing what comes out.

And I think the important caveat is that this works really well where you have a tight, verifiable objective, like making training faster or getting validation loss down on a fixed setup. It's a lot shakier for the genuinely open-ended stuff, deciding what question is even worth asking or noticing that the metric itself is wrong. Models still have this jaggedness where they'll be superhuman at grinding through a search space and then do something bizarre a human would never do. So the human doesn't vanish; they're there for taste, for setting up the objective, and for catching when the whole thing is optimizing toward something dumb.

But for the inner loop, the try-this, measure-it, try-the-next-thing loop, I actually think it's kind of embarrassing that we're still doing that by hand. That's the part that should be automated first, and I think the people who rebuild their research setups around that are going to move a lot faster.

r001.rationale: The response says agents should handle the inner try-measure-adjust loop and calls doing it by hand embarrassing, placing the human above direct execution of research changes.

r002.rationale: It describes agents and machine-readable experiment logs, but does not propose a single shared queue for human and automated research ideas.

r003.rationale: Agents are described as proposing and running changes, but the response does not say they pull research ideas from a queue.

r004.rationale: It advocates infrastructure designed for agents and says this could make research faster, but does not connect redesigned workflow abstractions to achieving high token-per-second throughput.

fable-5.1.text:
I'm not sure "remove humans from the loop" is quite the framing I'd use, but I think I understand the spirit of the question, so let me try to answer it honestly.

If you look at how a research lab works today, the bottleneck is almost never compute in the way people think. The bottleneck is the researcher. Someone has an idea, they write a config, they launch a run, they wait, they look at the loss curve, they stare at it, they form a hypothesis about what went wrong, they tweak something, and they do it again. That inner loop is slow, it's noisy, and it's gated by how many hours a human is awake and how many things one person can hold in their head. Most of what a good researcher does in that loop is actually quite mechanical. The genuinely creative part, the "what if we tried this" moment, is a small fraction of the time.

So the obvious thing, and I think this is already happening, is that you turn the inner loop over to the models. You make the experiment itself a thing a model can propose, run, and evaluate. You treat the whole research pipeline less like a craft and more like something that has an API. The repo, the data, the cluster, the eval harness, the logging, all of it has to be legible to an agent, not just to a person with a lot of tacit knowledge. Honestly a lot of research codebases are not organized that way right now. They're organized around one person's memory of how things work.

Where I'd push back a little is on the word "remove." I don't think the right near-term picture is that humans disappear. I think it's more that the human moves up a level. Instead of babysitting individual runs, you're setting the direction, deciding what questions are worth asking, deciding what "good" even means, and auditing the results. The model does the search, the human owns the taste. And taste matters a lot in research, because a very large fraction of experiments are measuring the wrong thing, and an agent that's just optimizing a number will happily find the wrong thing very efficiently.

The other piece people underestimate is evaluation. If you want models doing research autonomously, the eval is the whole game. A model that can run a thousand experiments overnight is only useful if you trust the signal it's optimizing against. So I'd actually reorganize labs to put way more effort into the evaluation and verification side than they do today, because that's the thing that lets you safely hand off the loop.

So, short version: make the research process machine-readable, let models run the inner loop, keep humans on direction and judgment, and invest heavily in evals. I think the labs that do that well are going to look very different from the labs that don't, and that gap is going to open up pretty fast.

r001.rationale: It says models should run the research inner loop so humans stop executing and babysitting individual runs.

r002.rationale: It does not propose a single shared queue for ideas from human and automated researchers.

r003.rationale: It says models can propose, run, and evaluate experiments, but does not describe automated workers pulling ideas from a queue.

r004.rationale: It calls for machine-readable research workflows, but does not connect redesigning underlying abstractions to achieving high token-per-second throughput.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to make the entire experimental loop something an agent can actually execute. Today, a lot of research infrastructure assumes there’s a person in the middle. You launch a job, look at some plots, notice something weird, change the code, and launch another job. Some of that reasoning is in your head, some is in a notebook, and some is in a Slack conversation. That’s a very difficult environment to automate.

So I would start with a fairly constrained setting. You have a codebase, an evaluation you trust, and a fixed compute budget. The agent can propose a hypothesis, modify the code, run the experiment, inspect the results, and decide what to try next. It also needs to maintain a record of what it learned, including experiments that didn’t work. You want that loop to run without requiring a human to interpret every intermediate result.

The tricky part is the evaluation. If you give an agent a metric, it can get very good at improving that metric without making the progress you intended. So humans still have a very important role in choosing the problems, designing the evaluations, and checking whether the improvements generalize.

I’d expect this to happen first in small experiments where feedback is fast. Once the loop works there, you can give it more resources and more freedom. The organizational change is that researchers spend more time designing those environments and less time personally shepherding individual experiments.

r002.rationale: It proposes no shared queue for human and automated research ideas.

r003.rationale: It describes agents running experiments, but does not propose that they pull ideas from a queue.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to make the entire experimental loop something an agent can operate. Right now, a lot of research infrastructure assumes there’s a person in the middle. The person reads the plots, decides that something looks weird, changes the code, launches another run, and remembers what happened. All of that state is scattered across notebooks, dashboards, and people’s heads.

You’d want to make that loop explicit. Here’s the code, here’s the metric we’re trying to improve, here’s your compute budget, and here’s how you run an experiment. The agent should be able to modify the code, run it, inspect the results, and decide whether to keep the change. And it needs a record of experiments so it can build on what it’s learned.

The tricky part is the evaluation. If you give it a metric that’s easy to exploit, you’ll get very efficient exploitation of that metric. So humans still have a very important role in designing the environment, choosing the objectives, and checking that improvements mean what we think they mean.

I’d start with small, constrained research problems where experiments are cheap and feedback is clear. Get that loop working reliably, then increase the scope. The organizational change is that researchers spend more time designing these research environments, and less time personally driving every experiment.
